blocks:
Fox's jaw tightens. He holds Elder Thorne's gaze, one hand resting on the worn leather of his bow strap.

"I read it." The words come out steadier than he feels. "Every sealed line. Every deliberate omission. The 'Great Caldera Event' — you left it undefined. That's not an accident, and you know it."

He takes a breath, forcing himself not to look away.

"The cipher, though... that's the part I can't shake. The letter-patterns. They match something I saw in the Hollow Archive. The section on Pre-Mortal Architecture." He lets that hang. "I don't know what it says yet. But I know it's older than the treaty. Older than this kingdom."

He tilts his head, a flicker of the old sharp curiosity breaking through.

"So tell me, Elder — what exactly did I read? Because you didn't chase me across three days of mountain passes just to scold a student for sneaking a peek."

Elder Thorne studies Fox for a long, silent moment, his papery fingers steepled beneath his chin. The candlelight carves deep shadows into the canyons of his face.

*"You came back. That took either great wisdom... or great foolishness. I haven't yet decided which."*

He rises slowly, crossing to a brass brazier where a few embers still glow. He doesn't look at Fox as he speaks.

*"Tell me, young one — when you read the cipher's last line, did you sound out the syllables of the pre-elf script aloud, or only in your head? The distinction matters more than you know."*

Fox meets Thorne's flint-gray gaze without flinching, though his fingers twitch at his sides — a betrayer's habit he's never quite mastered.

"I came back, didn't I?" *He lets the words hang, then shakes his head slowly.* "Three days. Iron Crossing, the Hollow Archive's outer shelves, a stopped clock in a traveler's inn, and a long walk back through the mist — all because of seven pages you left unlocked."

*He steps closer, voice dropping.*

"I memorized every word. The Great Caldera clause. The missing definition. The cipher at the bottom — the one written in a script that doesn't belong to any mortal kingdom. I don't know what it says, but I know *where* I've seen those letter-shapes before."

*He waits, letting that sink in.*

"Pre-Mortal Architecture. The forbidden section. You want to know what I think I saw? I think someone built that clause *before* we existed. And I think you already knew that."

Elder Thorne's papery fingers steeple on the scroll. The candlelight catches the silver threading in his robe, and for a long moment the only sound is the whisper of embers in the brazier.

*Finally, he speaks, his voice soft as dry leaves.*

"You were always the brightest of your cohort, Fox. Curious to a fault. I remember you at fifteen, copying the Great Caldera marginalia in the lower archives when you were supposed to be indexing tax ledgers."

*A pause. His flint eyes bore into you.*

"The cipher in the appendix's last line — it is not a code. It is a *lock*. One I helped place. What you read was never meant to be read by *anyone* outside the three signatories." *He leans forward, just slightly.* "Have you told another soul what you believe you deciphered?"

Fox's hand drifts unconsciously toward the ashwood bow slung across his back, then stops halfway — a twitch he doesn't quite suppress. He meets the Elder's flint eyes with his own, sharper and younger, but trying very hard not to seem like a cornered animal.

"Three days, yes. Give or take the night I spent trying to convince myself I'd imagined the whole thing." A dry, humorless smile. "I read it. Every word. The cipher at the bottom too — though I'll save you the trouble of asking: no, I haven't cracked it. Yet."

He lets the last word hang, a deliberate provocation, watching Thorne's face for the slightest crack in that serene elder mask.

Elder Thorne's papery fingers fold the message with precise, deliberate creases. The silver lantern on his desk casts your shadows long across the chamber floor. He does not sit. He does not dismiss you. 'Then we are bound,' he says, and the words settle like dust on old parchment. Outside the high windows, the white spires darken against a sky turning indigo. The silver lantern flickers once — a breath of air from nowhere — and the silence after his words is heavier than any argument. He has not summoned guards. He has not let you leave.
